contributions.method: FakeXplainer fine-tunes MLLMs using SFT followed by progressive GRPO; structured verdict, region-caption and tag outputs; and classification, output-format and bounding-box IoU rewards. The method contribution remains independently supported (Section 4, pp. 5–6).
contributions.dataset: FakeXplained contains 8,772 selected synthetic images with original region-caption and global-tag annotations. It is a separately named major contribution with detailed construction and quality control, annotation-component ablations, and demonstrated use for other detectors.
contributions.benchmark: The paper uses same-data four-fold accuracy/IoU comparisons and external out-of-distribution tests. These do not alone establish a separately substantive benchmark under R2. No additional benchmark type is proposed within this bounded R100/R1 review.

dataset_review.finding: The paper reports 8,772 original selected AI-generated images, without real images inside FakeXplained itself (Section 3.1, p. 4; Appendix A, p. 15; A.4, p. 18). It reports a mean of 5.42 region-caption pairs per image, not an exact total annotation count.

Section 3.1 (p. 4) states 28 generators across diffusion, GAN, DiT and other families. Table 1 (p. 8) names 27: 15 diffusion (DALL·E 2/3, DDIM, DDPM, FLUX.1-dev/schnell, GLIDE, Midjourney v4/v5, SD 1.4/1.5/2.1/3.5 Large/3.5 Large Turbo, VQDM); 4 GAN (BigGAN, GALIP, VQGAN, StyleGAN-XL); 4 DiT (PixArtAlpha/Delta/Sigma, DiT); 4 other (VAR, Infinity, MaskGIT, LlamaGen). This published discrepancy is unresolved. Per-generator image counts, seeds and checkpoint digests are not specified.

Section 3.1 (p. 4) describes generation across 1,000 ImageNet categories using a realistic-image/class-name prompt and MS COCO 2017 captions. Most images are 512×512; native 1024×1024 outputs are downsampled before annotation. Manual screening removes low-quality or unrecognizable examples and images described as having no real-looking part. Exact category/caption assignments, prompts, seeds and source-image identifiers are unavailable. Table 1’s real-image row cites ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), but exact real-image identifiers and sampling are not supplied.

Section 3.2 (p. 4) represents each region as (R_i,T_i): a rectangular box and associated text. Figures 2 (p. 3) and 8 (p. 18) illustrate textual integer-coordinate boxes emitted with captions inside structured reasoning. The reported mean is 5.42 box-caption pairs per image. An exact machine-readable file schema and coordinate normalization convention are not fully specified; actual annotation files were unavailable.

Section 3.2 (p. 4) and Appendix A.1 (p. 16) pair each box with a concise anomaly/artifact explanation. The instructions require a noun-led description confined to visible content in the selected region. Examples include physical/common-sense violations, repetitive patterns and illegible text. Figure 9 (p. 20) compares human and model region-caption examples.

Appendix A.1 (p. 16) defines six independently assignable tags: perspective errors, artistic styles, unknown objects, structure/attribute errors, texture errors and other anomalies. Images may receive zero or several tags. Rare or unfamiliar objects are not automatically impossible. Artistic style is an image-level judgment; a small local stylized part alone should not trigger it.

Section 3.2 (p. 4) reports 23 trained annotators. Appendix A.1 (pp. 15–16) describes prior photography experience, exposure to generated images, basic photographic literacy and a standardized handout with positive/negative examples and box/tag instructions. This establishes trained human annotators, not independently certified specialist credentials.

Sections 3.1–3.3 and Appendix A.1 describe manual image screening, human region/caption/tag annotation, manually curated control references and algorithmic IoU/tag checks. However, Section H (p. 22) explicitly says MLLMs generated or assisted annotation generation. The assisted stages, records, fraction, models and human verification are not quantified. It is therefore unsupported to call the entire dataset purely manual.

Section 3.3 (p. 5) and A.1 (p. 16) compare 5% of annotated images with research-team controls. An annotator’s preceding work is rejected if average box IoU is below 20% or tag agreement below 1/3; the fraction was visually verified, not misread as 13. Final control-reference IoU is 42.35% and tag agreement 79.67%. These are control-reference quality results, not formal all-pair inter-annotator agreement or kappa/alpha statistics. Caption reliability is not separately quantified.

Section 5.2 (p. 7) defines four-fold cross-validation: 75% synthetic images plus an equal number of real images for training; 25% synthetic images plus equal real images for testing. If all 8,772 images are divided exactly, arithmetic gives 6,579 synthetic training and 2,193 synthetic test images per fold; these are derived figures, not published index files. Separate validation indices, seeds, stratification, deduplication and SFT-versus-GRPO allocations are not fully specified. The 5% quality-control subset is annotation validation, not an independently specified model-validation partition. Earlier-preprint SFT/GRPO split percentages are not transferred to this version.

Table 3 (p. 8) and Table 6 (p. 19) evaluate FakeClue, Chameleon, GPT-Image-1, FaceForensics++ and MMFR (eval) as external detection datasets. They are not included in the original 8,772-image FakeXplained count. Table 3 reports accuracy of 85.2%, 84.3%, 80.1%, 86.4% and 87.4%, respectively. No external spatial ground truth or localization result is established there.

Section 5.1 (p. 7) trains ObjectFormer and SegFormer on FakeXplained, converting boxes into binary masks. Image classifiers use image-level labels. Table 2 (p. 8) also uses several MLLM backbones. This demonstrates that the annotated resource can support architectures other than FakeXplainer, independently of its proposed method. Actual outside-team reuse cannot be verified without released assets.

The abstract claims code and data are available at the author-linked Gennadiyev/FakeXplain repository. On 2026-10-21, GitHub HTML explicitly showed an empty repository; repository metadata returned HTTP 200, size 0, license null and last push 2026-02-14T03:10:49Z; the contents endpoint returned HTTP 404 with an explicit empty-repository message. No README, annotation files, splits, data, dataset license or commit could be inspected. This is a point-in-time failure to verify release at the supplied link, not proof that no alternative authorized release exists. No alternative assets were sought.

Table 4 (p. 9): full model 98.2% accuracy/36.0% IoU, BLEU-2 0.267 and ROUGE-L 0.251; no-box 95.2% accuracy; no-caption 94.2% accuracy/26.5% IoU; no-tags 96.2% accuracy/35.8% IoU; label-only 93.7% accuracy. Table 6 gives label-only external accuracy 60.3%/64.0%/61.2% versus full 80.1%/86.4%/87.4% on GPT-Image-1/FF++/MMFR. These ablate annotation components. They are not a controlled substitute-dataset experiment: FakeShield uses pretrained weights and LEGION uses SynthScars.

Fully realistic synthetic images lacking visible flaws are explicitly outside the authors’ stated scope (Section 6, p. 10; Appendix F, p. 22).

current_canonical_bibliographic_record.abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and diffusion models significantly enhances the realism of synthetic images, driving progress in image processing and creative design. However, this progress also necessitates the development of effective detection methods, as synthetic images become increasingly difficult to distinguish from real ones. This difficulty leads to various societal issues, such as the spread of misinformation, identity theft, and online fraud. While previous detection methods perform well on public benchmarks, they struggle with our proposed benchmark, FakeART, particularly when dealing with the latest models and cross-domain tasks (e.g., photo-to-painting). To address this challenge, we develop a new synthetic image detection technique based on color distribution. Unlike real images, synthetic images often exhibit uneven color distribution. By employing color quantization and restoration techniques, we analyze the color differences before and after image restoration. We discover and prove that these differences closely relate to the uniformity of color distribution. Based on this finding, we extract effective color features and combine them with image features to create a detection model with only 1.4 million parameters. This model achieves state-of-the-art results across various evaluation benchmarks, including the challenging FakeART dataset.

While previous detection methods perform well on public benchmarks, they struggle with our proposed benchmark, FakeART, particularly when dealing with the latest models and cross-domain tasks (e.g., photo-to-painting). To address this challenge, we develop a new synthetic image detection technique based on color distribution. Unlike real images, synthetic images often exhibit uneven color distribution. By employing color quantization and restoration techniques, we analyze the color differences before and after image restoration. We discover and prove that these differences closely relate to the uniformity of color distribution. Based on this finding, we extract effective color features and combine them with image features to create a detection model with only 1.4 million parameters. This model achieves state-of-the-art results across various evaluation benchmarks, including the challenging FakeART dataset.

canonical.title: FakeXplain: AI-Generated Image Detection via Human-Aligned Grounded Reasoning
canonical.authors: Yikun Ji, Yan Hong, Qi Fan, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Liqing Zhang, Jianfu Zhang
canonical.abstract: The rapid rise of image generation calls for detection methods that are both interpretable and reliable. Existing approaches, though accurate, act as black boxes and fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data, while multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) provide reasoning ability but often hallucinate. To address these issues, we construct FakeXplained dataset of AI-generated images annotated with bounding boxes and descriptive captions that highlight synthesis artifacts, forming the basis for human-aligned, visually grounded reasoning. Leveraging FakeXplained, we develop FakeXplainer which fine-tunes MLLMs with a progressive training pipeline, enabling accurate detection, artifact localization, and coherent textual explanations. Extensive experiments show that FakeXplainer not only sets a new state-of-the-art in detection and localization accuracy (98.2% accuracy, 36.0% IoU), but also demonstrates strong robustness and out-of-distribution generalization, uniquely delivering spatially grounded, human-aligned rationales. The code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/Gennadiyev/FakeXplain.

canonical.abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and diffusion models significantly enhances the realism of synthetic images, driving progress in image processing and creative design. However, this progress also necessitates the development of effective detection methods, as synthetic images become increasingly difficult to distinguish from real ones. This difficulty leads to various societal issues, such as the spread of misinformation, identity theft, and online fraud. While previous detection methods perform well on public benchmarks, they struggle with our proposed benchmark, FakeART, particularly when dealing with the latest models and cross-domain tasks (e.g., photo-to-painting). To address this challenge, we develop a new synthetic image detection technique based on color distribution. Unlike real images, synthetic images often exhibit uneven color distribution. By employing color quantization and restoration techniques, we analyze the color differences before and after image restoration. We discover and prove that these differences closely relate to the uniformity of color distribution. Based on this finding, we extract effective color features and combine them with image features to create a detection model with only 1.4 million parameters. This model achieves state-of-the-art results across various evaluation benchmarks, including the challenging FakeART dataset.

curated:411724cd949b78c1af6a.abstract: The rapid rise of image generation calls for detection methods that are both interpretable and reliable. Existing approaches, though accurate, act as black boxes and fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data, while multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) provide reasoning ability but often hallucinate. To address these issues, we construct FakeXplained dataset of AI-generated images annotated with bounding boxes and descriptive captions that highlight synthesis artifacts, forming the basis for human-aligned, visually grounded reasoning. Leveraging FakeXplained, we develop FakeXplainer which fine-tunes MLLMs with a progressive training pipeline, enabling accurate detection, artifact localization, and coherent textual explanations. Extensive experiments show that FakeXplainer not only sets a new state-of-the-art in detection and localization accuracy (98.2% accuracy, 36.0% IoU), but also demonstrates strong robustness and out-of-distribution generalization, uniquely delivering spatially grounded, human-aligned rationales. The code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/Gennadiyev/FakeXplain.
